Networks (TCNs) are well-suited for processing time-series data. However, optimizing the time-dilated convolution in TCNs typically involves a trial-and-error approach. We've developed an automatic optimizer that tackles this challenge by treating dilation factor selection as a weight pruning problem on the time-axis. Our method learns dilation factors alongside model weights during training, leading to significant memory reductions and computation savings on real-world audio classification datasets without compromising accuracy.

using convolutional neural networks (CNNs) has gained significant attention. Two primary categories of approaches have emerged: direct methods and two-stage pipelines that utilize intermediate cues. In the latter category, CNNs first predict intermediate cues such as 3D object coordinates or virtual control points, from which the object pose is derived. This paper focuses on refining two-stage pipelines by integrating two distinct concepts: dual-task learning and multi-object pose estimation. We propose training a network to predict not just a single object pose, but rather multiple object poses simultaneously. Furthermore, each pose is defined by two 3D points instead of a full 3D bounding box, which provides more flexibility in data generation and allows for the explicit representation of pose ambiguities. Moreover, we augment the network with an additional branch that predicts 3D object coordinates from the predicted poses, serving as a dual task. Through extensive experiments on three public datasets, we demonstrate the superiority of our approach over existing two-stage pipelines and certain direct methods. However, we find that direct regression methods still outperform our proposal on certain evaluation metrics.

The most effective methods were identified and their strengths were clarified within the framework of an idealized test. For harmonic oscillators, certain high-order methods demonstrated the ability to maintain accuracy even when paired with MTS, whereas for more complex systems involving bond stretching, "optimal" methods were found to depend on the degree of MTS. In general, MTS schemes performed better when paired with lower-order methods than with higher-order ones. Various methods exist for generating these initial conditions, which can affect the final outcome of the simulation. In this study, we examine how different initial conditions influence the final result for a specific simulation of a black hole binary with a dark matter halo. All the conditions we tested produced similar results, but they diverged from a previous set of results produced by another group of researchers. Through the examination of extensive categories of Type IIB four-dimensional $\mathcal{N}=2$ effective field theories, we identify the potential generalized global symmetries present and investigate the mechanisms that circumvent them. Key components of such effective field theories include generalized $\theta$-terms, which introduce non-linear interactions between axion fields and topological terms that are quadratic in gauge field strengths and lead to the breaking of numerous global symmetries. Furthermore, assuming the presence of charged states can lead to the breaking of residual global symmetries. However, we demonstrate that the presence of generalized $\theta$-terms results in a generalized Witten effect, implying that the spectrum of charged states is composed of an infinitely populated grid. Consequently, this grid can be used to infer the structure of the effective operator governing the coupling between axions and gauge field strengths.

  Our objective is to minimize the amount of trust necessary in the hardware and software underlying a mobile system by partitioning resources securely without relying on existing components. We achieve this through a novel hardware component, a Trust-Enhanced Transactional System (TETS), integrating with existing hardware to safely isolate security-sensitive applications. TETS comprises two main components:
  1. A transactional memory system featuring hardware transactions securely shared between user and security applications, with user memory accessed through secure enclaves when possible.
  2. A multi-domain critical section (CDCS) system allowing multiple programs to concurrently execute critical sections without hardware intervention.
We demonstrate that by combining these two components, we can efficiently support various security APIs, including mutexes, semaphores, and atomic instructions, while also enabling programming languages to safely utilize TETS through transactional memory and synchronization libraries with minimal overhead.
In collaboration with researchers from Harvard University and University of Illinois at Chicago, we have successfully implemented TETS on an Intel Skylake chip using Intel Software Guard Extensions (SGX) to create a proof-of-concept transactional memory system and CDCS hardware components.
Our evaluation using a transactional memory compiler and security-sensitive applications shows that performance overhead is comparable to current state-of-the-art transactional memory designs, with some programs experiencing little to no slowdown.

scenarios where an adaptive adversary intentionally manipulates reward and transition data. The adversary's influence is bounded by a fraction $\eta$ of all possible actions, affecting the perceived reward and transition probabilities. Notably, this model allows for situations where the attack is focused on a specific subset of episodes. Our main finding is that no reinforcement learning algorithm can achieve a policy better than $O(\eta)$ in terms of expected cumulative reward when faced with an unbounded number of episodes and an adversary that can influence each episode independently. However, we developed a novel algorithm, Robust Q-learning, which can achieve a policy that is at most $O(\eta^2)$ suboptimal under certain conditions and performs significantly better than Q-learning in our theoretical and practical evaluations. Furthermore, we found that the sample complexity of Robust Q-learning grows quadratically with the number of episodes, indicating that robust reinforcement learning may require a larger number of training episodes to generalize effectively. To overcome this limitation, we explored an alternative algorithm that utilizes an additional set of clean episodes to improve its performance.

multi-phonon physics, is being explored for its potential in metrology and on-chip communication, among other applications. Quantum acoustic resonators, or cavities, are being utilized to investigate multi-phonon phenomena through both theoretical and experimental means. We are studying a specific system consisting of a semiconductor quantum dot driven by a laser, coupled to an acoustic cavity. This setup has shown promise in producing interesting multi-phonon effects, but a previous model of the quantum dot as a two-level system was too restrictive. In this work, we instead consider a model that accounts for both bright and dark excitons in the quantum dot, with dark excitons being particularly useful due to their low decoherence rates. By fine-tuning the laser frequency, we are able to achieve giant Rabi oscillations between the vacuum state and a dark exciton state accompanied by N-phonon bundles. Notably, we can create dark states in the quantum dot without the need for an external magnetic field, and in a scenario with losses, the system acts as a phonon gun capable of emitting N-phonon bundles.

lattice from a non-symmorphic wallpaper group, specifically the herringbone lattice with two orthogonal glide symmetries. We model this system using a nearest-neighbour tight-binding model and find two distinct Dirac cones within the first Brillouin zone along a high-symmetry path. These Dirac cones can be modified through various perturbations applied to the Hamiltonian, which break the lattice symmetries. Initially, we explore how these cones can be transformed into semi-Dirac or nodal-line states by introducing sublattice asymmetry or specific onsite potentials. Secondly, we analyze how a dimeric next-nearest-neighbour hopping interaction affects the Dirac cones, resulting in a transition from quasi-flat to nodal-line states along certain high-symmetry directions. Additionally, we reveal that the nodal lines can be curved into a more complex 3D structure, an isolated zero-energy point, or a higher-order zero-energy point within the energy spectrum.

yzed coherent states (SPCCSs) can be generated through a process called quantum-optical catalysis using beam splitters or parametric amplifiers. This occurs when a coherent state and a single-photon state are input into a beam splitter or parametric amplifier, and a single photon is detected in one of the output channels. The probabilities of successful detection differ depending on whether a beam splitter or parametric amplifier is used. We have fully characterized two types of SPCCSs - even SPCCSs and binomial SPCCSs - by analyzing their photon number distributions. The study of these states can be used to investigate nonclassical effects such as sub-Poisson distribution, quadrature squeezing, and anti-bunching. Notably, the sub-Poisson distribution of even SPCCSs can be controlled by adjusting the ratio of coherent field amplitudes.

CT scans can be very difficult due to low contrast, varying anatomy, and the presence of foreign objects. To overcome this, doctors often rely on additional information from endoscopic findings, medical history, and other imaging tests, which can be time-consuming and produce inconsistent results. In this study, we investigate the potential of a simplified, fully automated computer system for identifying esophageal tumors in CT scans. The system uses a technique called region growing to identify tumors and then evaluates the results against a large set of patient images with annotated tumors. The results show that this approach can produce accurate tumor identifications with a high degree of consistency.

, and hydrocarbons are frequently discovered in intricate reservoir formations. To optimize production from such reservoirs and minimize costs, precise well placement in real-time is essential. This process, known as geosteering, is typically supported by up-to-date formation evaluations obtained through well-log interpretation while drilling. For this application, a reliable, computationally efficient, and robust workflow to analyze well logs and capture uncertainties in real-time is necessary. An iterative ensemble-based method, specifically the approximate Levenberg Marquardt form of the Ensemble Randomized Maximum Likelihood (LM-EnRML), has been adopted in this study for forming accurate probabilistic models of well logs. The proposed method iteratively refines a probabilistic formation model by minimizing the discrepancy between measured data and theoretical values obtained from the forward simulation of geophysical reservoir models. A key aspect of this study involves assessing the statistical model's reliability through the analysis of the ensemble's autocorrelation and cross-covariance matrices. Moreover, the proposed method is computationally efficient due to its limited number of required reservoir model realizations and iterations, making it suitable for real-time geosteering. The developed statistical model's reliability and computational efficiency are demonstrated through a synthetic case study and a real-field data example.

One type of NER, nested NER, focuses on recognizing entities within other entities. Most existing nested NER studies apply linear models, which are challenging to scale to complex, real-world applications. To address this limitation, we propose a new framework that utilizes a pre-trained language model to model non-linear relationships and learn rich contextual representations. Our framework, which incorporates a type-aware attention mechanism and a nested information mask, enables the detection of nested entities by leveraging both entity types and subword information. Experimental results on benchmark datasets demonstrate the effectiveness of our approach, achieving significant improvements over existing baseline models.

When communicating, they may blend languages, also known as code-switching or code-mixing, by switching between different languages within a single utterance. This research explores current NLP developments, constraints, and potential obstacles for creating innovative NLP tools catering to multilingual communities that engage in code-switching. We examine various NLP applications, including text classification, sentiment analysis, and machine translation, and provide an overview of relevant corpus resources and statistical models that can be utilized for monolingual and multilingual NLP tasks. We discuss the challenges posed by code-switching, limited corpus resources, and excessive noise when attempting to build practical NLP solutions. We also suggest potential future research avenues for developers, researchers, and practitioners to develop more effective NLP tools for the multilingual community.

Our primary objective is to elucidate how the widespread use of embeddings in NLP is influenced by the distribution of terms within a given corpus. We utilize a mathematical framework to highlight the implicit assumptions regarding language structure inherent in this model. Our analysis reveals that Markovian assumptions provide a clear theoretical understanding of how embeddings are formed and how they capture frequentist synonyms. These assumptions enable the creation of generative models and an explicit analysis of the common pitfalls associated with the widespread use of word2vec. We also introduce a new metric, called the relative frequency quotient, which offers valuable insights into understanding the complex relationships between terms within a corpus. This metric enables the distinction between frequentist and distributional synonyms and provides a clear theoretical justification for the widespread use of embeddings in NLP. We demonstrate the efficacy of our proposed metric through various experiments conducted on diverse corpora, including scientific and informal texts, as well as translations. Our results show that the most similar terms to a given term, based on its embeddings, are not necessarily the top terms that appear in the distribution of a corpus. We also highlight the complex relationships between terms within a corpus and provide a set of recommendations for the prudent use of embeddings in NLP.

the Milky Way's center that have shown no outbursts in over a decade have led researchers to categorize them as "X-ray quiescent" despite being detected in surveys. By identifying these sources and understanding their characteristics, researchers can make various astrophysical connections, such as determining the population of binary systems containing an intermediate-mass black hole or assessing the likelihood of an ultralight dark matter field. A comprehensive study of these sources is essential to avoid biased conclusions about this population. This study classifies X-ray quiescent variables as either those with confirmed or likely companions or those with no confirmed or likely companions. The former group includes systems with an established or suspected mass transfer, such as magnetic binaries or those with a white dwarf or neutron star companion. The latter group includes systems with no detected outburst and no indication of an active galaxy nucleus, but also those with no detected companion and no known counterpart at other wavelengths. The study finds that the majority of X-ray quiescent variables with confirmed or likely companions are found in the central 0.3 deg^2 of the Galaxy and that some of these likely companions are binary systems with a low-mass companion. Furthermore, the study estimates that the density of systems with an intermediate-mass black hole in the Galaxy's center is less than 10^4 deg^-3.

To this end, I examined the feasibility of using the velocity dispersion of binary star systems from the catalogue of Evans et al. (2019a), focusing on reducing potential sources of error. It was determined that the main contaminants to precise velocity dispersion measurements are binary star systems with uncertain or wide velocity distributions, as well as those influenced by moving groups or the Galactic bar. By applying strict filtering criteria to eliminate these contaminants and accounting for residual scatter, the accuracy of velocity dispersion measurements was significantly improved. Under these conditions, the standard model of binary star velocity distributions yielded a best-fit parameter value for the acceleration at which gravity loses dominance, with an associated error of $10^{-10} \, M_{\odot}^{-1} \, {\rm km}^3 \, {\rm s}^{-2}$. This value is consistent with a similar analysis of satellite data, but with larger error margins.

Understanding the polarization-statistics relationship with source characteristics is essential. By analyzing large radio source samples from 1.4 GHz surveys, researchers found correlations between polarization and flux-density, spectral-index, and source-size. A second, less pronounced trend emerges at higher polarization levels, where there's a positive correlation with flux-density. The underlying mechanisms for these interactions are magnetic field distribution, particle energy-spectra, and the orientation of radio-source asymmetry.

We have developed a numerical model to examine the effects of angular momentum on the development of sustainable hydrogen burning in stars with masses below 0.26 solar masses. By simulating the behavior of these objects with varying levels of angular momentum, our results demonstrate that those with sufficient angular momentum will experience mass loss due to their rapid rotation, creating a stable relationship between their spin period and mass that resembles that of pulsational binary systems. Conversely, objects with lower angular momentum will be subject to gravitational contraction, and those with very low angular momentum may undergo significant mass loss before entering the sustainable burning phase. Our findings also indicate that sustainable hydrogen burning may only occur within a specific range of spin periods in objects with masses around 0.19 solar masses.

observed in 1979 that over finite fields $k$, the total residue map $\text{res}$ from Laurent series to $k$ is expressible in a specific language involving power series and their derivatives. This paper demonstrates that $\text{THF}$ does not have the approximation property, and subsequently, it is shown that the power series field with a total residue map is not axiomatizable by a decidable theory. research introduces a new technique called HyperDegrade, which combines existing methods with a new strategy called simultaneous multithreading (SMT).  Our study reveals that HyperDegrade is significantly more effective than current techniques in extracting sensitive information from a CPU-based side-channel.  To achieve this level of performance, we developed a new profiling method called multi-exponential decay (MED) model, which enables the detection of distinct execution paths with high precision.  Our measurements demonstrate that HyperDegrade can successfully identify execution paths even when using an unoptimized software.  To further evaluate the effectiveness of HyperDegrade, we conducted a user-space attack on an out-of-order CPU, which resulted in the complete disclosure of a 128-bit AES encryption key.  This new technique offers a notable improvement in side-channel exploitation, reducing the required computational time by approximately 10 to 50 times compared to existing methods.

Although the Standard Model (SM) contribution of the Higgs to the muon's magnetic dipole moment is minimal, a bottom-up EFT analysis reveals that the Higgs could still resolve the anomaly if its interactions with other SM particles deviate from their predicted values. Applying unitarity principles, we found that such a solution would imply the presence of New Physics at an energy scale of around 10-18 TeV, which could be lowered to 5 TeV if the Higgs interactions with the W and Z bosons conform to SM expectations. as an unknotting operation. Any given knot diagram can be transformed into a trivial unknot diagram by applying a series of unknotting operations in conjunction with some Reidemeister moves. Unknotting operations hold considerable significance in the field of knot theory as they facilitate the analysis of knot complexity and invariants. Moreover, they also have substantial applications in biology, chemistry, and physics for studying intricate string entanglements, organic compound structures, and DNA configurations. In this research, we developed a novel unknotting procedure that utilizes a specific set of operations to disembed a knot's crossing in a step-by-step manner. The number of operations required to disembed the knot is directly correlated with the crossing number of the knot. The study also introduces a set of diagrams for the figure-eight knot that necessitate the minimum number of operations to disembed a crossing, which is three. This process involves six operations that remove sixteen crossings, ten double points, and four triple points.

Fields like computer graphics, graph theory, and machine learning heavily rely on matrices to solve their respective problems.
Given the frequency of matrix operations, efficient matrix handling is crucial for algorithm performance.
One of the most commonly used matrix operations is multiplication, which can become a bottleneck in computational performance as matrix size increases.
As a result, parallel computing has become a standard solution to tackle this issue.
This report presents a comparison between sequential and parallel approaches to matrix multiplication using CUDA and openMP.
The results of the analysis demonstrate the importance of parallelization, particularly for large matrices where computational time is significantly reduced.

This study examines how a group of rational agents decide which tasks to undertake when some tasks are only feasible by combining efforts. We find that the set of jointly feasible tasks grows exponentially with the number of agents, creating an information overload that hinders cooperation. To address this, we introduce a heuristic in which each agent prioritizes tasks based on their value and the number of other agents involved, resulting in a distributed strategy that yields a significant reduction in the complexity of feasible options. Through simulations, we show that this heuristic leads to a substantial increase in the likelihood of achieving jointly feasible tasks and a notable improvement in overall payoff.

study, we concentrate on vertical federated learning (VFL), which allows multiple entities to jointly train a robust machine learning model using shared features, without exchanging sensitive information. Based on collaboration patterns, VFL can be categorized into two main types: end-to-end collaboration and intermediate collaboration. The former involves entities directly exchanging encrypted data with each other, while the latter involves entities exchanging decrypted data with a semi-trusted coordinator. Although the latter has been gaining attention due to its potential to overcome communication constraints and data privacy limitations, research on intermediate collaboration VFL is still in its infancy. Specifically, existing schemes lack robustness against malicious entities and have significant computational overhead. To address these issues, we propose a novel framework for intermediate collaboration VFL, which incorporates multi-task learning to enhance model security and employs hash-based data aggregation to reduce computational costs. Our proposed framework also outperforms existing VFL solutions in terms of model accuracy and computational efficiency.

To address this limitation, Random Fourier Features (RFF) were introduced as a method to approximate kernel functions using randomized Fourier features, thereby enabling the use of kernel methods on large datasets. Although RFF has gained popularity, it still has significant drawbacks, particularly the need for a large number of feature expansions that is directly proportional to the dataset size. This necessitates the use of dimensionality reduction techniques to achieve meaningful performance improvements, thereby introducing additional complexity. The proposed approach is extensively evaluated and compared with other kernel approximation methods on classification and regression tasks, showcasing its superior performance and scalability.

Tetralogy of Fallot patients primarily relies on heart volume and function, according to current guidelines. These biomarkers change noticeably in response to the surgery and can be accurately measured using magnetic resonance imaging. By analyzing recent studies, researchers found that using machine learning models like Generalized Enhanced Grid Search on various imaging data from these patients consistently produced highly reliable predictions for the need for surgery based on their heart images alone. Notably, these models performed better than more traditional approaches like multiple linear regression. To make surgery timing decisions more patient-specific and accountable, researchers developed an explainable version of the machine learning model, which identified key imaging features and individual patient factors that influence the decision. Furthermore, by reversing the model, they were able to identify specific changes in heart images that indicate the need for surgery. This work paves the way for using machine learning based on medical images to improve personalized management of common heart conditions.

Pyramid Networks (FPNs), have been facing a long-standing challenge. Research has been ongoing to address the performance gap between FPN-based detectors and non-FPN counterparts, such as two-stage detectors. This study aims to bridge this understanding gap by examining the underlying reasons for this performance disparity. We delve into the analysis of FPN's mechanism, detection framework's geometry, and optimization dynamics to identify the root causes. Based on these findings, we propose the FPN Detectors' Performance Gap Analysis Framework, which provides comprehensive insights. Furthermore, we derive actionable strategies to mitigate the performance gap. Notably, our empirical findings concur with our analytical results, and we also present practical solutions that can enhance detector performance.

conditionally specified models, which rely on implicit assumptions at their boundaries. Unfortunately, current methodologies lack a systematic approach to assess these extreme assumptions due to complex, intractable bounds. In this research, we develop a novel method that utilizes sampling algorithms and empirical likelihood to create a tractable, closed-form expression for the distribution of extreme values in multi-dimensional data. This enables us to evaluate and refine implicit assumptions at the boundaries of conditional models. We demonstrate the applicability and benefits of our method with three significant models: a latent variable model, an econophysics model, and a statistical physics model. Our results show that extreme assumptions are often over-optimistic, highlighting the necessity of extreme value theory in model accuracy. We also introduce Rmixtools (R package for model selection and estimation in mixture models) which incorporates our method to improve robustness.

Researchers have traditionally focused on removing nodes with the highest degree or betweenness centrality, but these methods can be ineffective, especially in scale-free networks. Given an irreducible simple algebraic group G and a Borel subgroup B, consider an irreducible subgroup P containing B, and let P' be its derived group. A theorem by Richardson states that the algebra of P semi-invariants is multiplicity-free. A linear subvariety e+V that induces an isomorphism between the algebra of P semi-invariants and the algebra of e+V is called a Weierstrass section. In this work, a Weierstrass section is constructed in type A, with a focus on its application rather than its construction. A description of the Weierstrass section is provided using the structure of the nilfibre, which is itself determined in the paper. The construction of a Weierstrass section has the potential to be generalised to other simple algebraic groups.

Researchers have developed alternative architectures like linear networks with a vast number of parameters, training linear models on a vast amount of data to achieve outstanding results. Nonetheless, these models often overlook the implicit relationships inherent in the data's structural matrix, which can be costly to estimate accurately. To address this limitation, a novel framework called Structurally Rich Linear Networks (SRLN) has been proposed, incorporating a non-parametric estimator for the structural matrix. By training the linear model using an unbiased estimator and minimizing the expected squared loss, the SRLN framework offers a transparent method that provides a comprehensive understanding of the data's underlying structure and simultaneously estimates a massive linear model. biolabs and infectious-control hospitals must meet stringent safety standards set by bio-safety levels (BSLs) to prevent potentially deadly pathogens from escaping into the surrounding environment. These facilities maintain negative air pressure relative to the outside space by closing off airflow with specialized doors and using variable frequency drives (VFDs) to regulate airflow. Modern control systems utilize feedback loops that compare pressure readings with predetermined safety levels, issuing commands to adjust VFDs and ensure NPRs' air pressure remains adequate. This implementation, however, has a significant flaw: it lacks inherent safety. During system failures, such as power outages or software crashes, the control software can become disabled, leading to unauthorized entry of the surrounding environment by harmful microorganisms. Researchers have developed a novel method to enhance NPRs' safety by incorporating a safety-critical control system using a state feedback controller with a built-in fail-safe mechanism, which ensures the facility meets BSL requirements even in the event of a control system failure. This innovative control system, housed in a separate, independent computer system, provides a certificate of compliance that documents its safety and reliability. By utilizing this modern control system, the risk of bio-safety level violations is minimized, and the NPR can be trusted to operate safely with minimal human intervention.

This paper explores the integration of IRS into radar systems, focusing on cross-section enhancement and target range estimation. By applying optimization techniques to adjust the radar and IRS parameters, the radar cross-section of an undetectable target can be increased, and the range of a detectable target can be accurately estimated. Numerical simulations demonstrate the effectiveness of IRS in enhancing radar cross-sections and estimating target ranges.

of dense suspensions undergo a sudden and dramatic transformation in their flow behavior, characterized by an abrupt thickening. This phenomenon is believed to be a precursor to a rigidity transition, triggered by a shift in the dominant interaction between suspended particles from hydrodynamic to frictional forces. Our research provides a comprehensive theory of viscosity, describing its behavior as a universal function that bridges the frictionless jamming point to a rigidity transition influenced by friction, anisotropy, and shear. Experimental evidence from two distinct systems - cornstarch in glycerol and silica spheres in glycerol - demonstrates that viscosity can be condensed into a single, universal curve spanning a broad range of stresses and volume fractions. The resulting collapse reveals two distinct scaling regimes, each with unique critical exponents, indicating that frictionless isotropic jamming and frictional shear jamming belong to separate universality classes. By incorporating material-specific behavior into a scaling variable that gauges proximity to shear jamming, our reformulation enables the application of established theoretical frameworks for equilibrium critical phenomena to elucidate fundamental physical aspects of the shear thickening transition.

Sketch maps vectors to lower dimensions using randomized linear measurements, allowing for the recovery of significant vector components. However, the stability of the sketch under noisy measurements is a significant concern. Research has been conducted to enhance the stability of the CountSketch sketch, particularly for sparse vectors with a limited number of large elements. The current study builds upon this work by developing a more resilient CountSketch sketch that can accurately recover the top-k elements of a vector even in the presence of a significant amount of noise. Unlike previous sketches, this one is stable for vectors with a limited condition number. The proposed sketch achieves a better recovery guarantee for sparse vectors, offering more stable performance and a higher level of accuracy. The noise tolerance of the sketch is directly proportional to the square root of the vector size, making it a more scalable option. The current study also provides a method for estimating the condition number of a vector from linear measurements. Theoretical results demonstrate that the recovery guarantee of the sketch can be improved through a more stringent stability criterion, allowing for a more accurate recovery of the top-k elements. The study also conducts a comprehensive analysis of various recovery algorithms, providing worst-case performance guarantees and empirical results. The proposed sketch has been applied in a practical setting, where it has been used to develop a more accurate algorithm for heavy-hitters detection in data streams with a limited memory size.

strategic deployment of aggregators that can efficiently convey their flexible capabilities, referred to as aggregate flexibility, to system operators. Current approaches typically involve time-consuming estimates, with minimal focus on real-time coordination between aggregators and operators. This paper proposes a solution to an online optimization problem within a closed-loop system by introducing a real-time feedback mechanism. Specifically, we train machine learning models on historical data to rapidly predict the entire distribution of individual aggregators' flexible capabilities (i.e., their own or those they control). By expanding the Einstein equations in terms of transverse gradients, it's found that numerical results match exact solutions at the first order of expansion. The Einstein equations at this order can be broken down into two sets of differential equations, where one set's bulk fields contribute negligibly to boundary observables. The framework achieves a significant speedup of roughly one order of magnitude, with errors of less than 10% at the hydrodynamization time and for low to mid rapidities.

The object's drag was found to behave differently at low and high Reynolds numbers, with a sudden change in drag occurring when the Reynolds number passed through a critical value. This phenomenon is similar to the drag crisis observed in fluid dynamics, but with a more dramatic effect. The transition from skin friction-dominated drag to turbulent flow-dominated drag is explained by the shift from a flow regime dominated by the object's geometric scale to one dominated by the granular bed's scale. The drag coefficients at the transition points are found to be comparable to those in fluid dynamics, but the Reynolds number at which the transition occurs is significantly lower. The ratio of the granular bed's scale to the object's scale strongly influences the drag transition, with a ratio of around 100 needed to observe the drag crisis. The flow patterns observed in the transition regions provide valuable insights into the transition mechanisms.

we've analyzed the large-scale structure of ionized and molecular gas in the starbursting galaxy IRAS08339+6517, located 500 parsecs in size. Our study has uncovered a direct relationship between the mass flux of star formation-driven gas outflows and the galaxy's star formation rate. The data suggest that outflows are closely linked to the galaxy's ability to recycle gas, with areas of high star formation rates expelling more gas than they consume through star formation. These findings support the idea that outflows play a crucial role in regulating the galaxy's ability to sustain short gas depletion times.

time-dependent partial differential equations (PDEs) lies in maintaining the integrity of specific properties inherent to the continuous solution, such as underlying conservation laws or geometric structures. Researchers have a rich history of developing and analyzing structure-preserving discretization techniques, including conservative finite differences, differential algebraic methods for Hamiltonian ODEs, and geometric integrators for ordinary differential equations (ODEs). However, the general framework for structure-preserving discretization methods has primarily focused on ordinary differential equations (ODEs), with less attention given to differential equations involving time-delays. This paper aims to fill this gap by exploring the construction and analysis of an explicit, high-order scheme for a broad class of differential equations with constant delays, which is widely applicable to time-dependent PDEs in their semi-discrete form. The proposed scheme maintains the underlying conservation law property and has a demonstrated order of convergence of two or higher, depending on the order of interest. The paper also presents a specific example by discretizing a popular model for stock prices with delays, providing numerical convergence evidence for two different initial conditions.

ubble evolution driven by young coeval massive star clusters within low-metallicity molecular clouds. Our research focuses on the early stages of superbubble evolution, including pair-instability and core-collapse supernovae. We aimed to investigate the growth of dust grains within orbiting dusty clumps and the superbubble's swept-up supershell, as well as the survival of dust grains produced by sequential supernovae. Our model accounts for the gravitational interaction between the cluster, clumps, and the supershell, as well as stellar feedback and radiative cooling. We followed the evolution of the superbubble until the first pair-instability supernova or core-collapse supernova. Our findings show that in large clusters, pair-instability supernovae occur before the superbubble becomes large enough for dust grains to be distributed throughout the surrounding cloud. Conversely, in small clusters, core-collapse supernovae create more dust than pair-instability supernovae, allowing for the growth of dust grains within orbiting clumps and contributing to the supershell's substantial dust content. This process results in an increased dust-to-gas ratio within the superbubble's swept-up supershell, making dust an important contributor to the total dust budget of the surrounding cloud.

To ensure safe braking distances, it is essential to detect obstacles beyond a certain range. However, existing benchmarks, such as the nuScenes dataset, do not adequately address this problem as they only evaluate performance up to a certain distance. This is partly due to the difficulty in obtaining accurate annotations for far-field objects, particularly with lidar sensors that often produce few point returns for distant objects. Moreover, current evaluation metrics for 3D detection are not tailored to the specific needs of far-field objects, which can lead to an incomplete analysis of this task. For instance, the conventional wisdom that high-resolution RGB sensors are essential for detecting far-away objects has been disputed by recent results showing that lidar-based methods still perform better on current benchmark leaderboards. To address this gap, we have developed a method for accurately annotating far-field objects in the nuScenes dataset and proposed a new evaluation protocol for 3D detection in complex outdoor scenes. Our experiments demonstrate the importance of distinguishing between near-field and far-field objects in 3D detection and provide insights into the relative difficulty of detecting far-field objects of different sizes.

Our model outperforms competing quantum neural network architectures in a benchmark test involving the prediction of energy values.

The choice between these methods depends on the particle's properties, as well as those of the detector used. To better understand the effectiveness of these methods, we are exploring how they interact with each other. This study examines how the ability to detect neutral long-lived particles that primarily leave behind missing energy in their decays is affected by the detection of additional final state particles and photons. We found that in certain cases, the ability to detect these particles is significantly enhanced when additional particles are present, and this complementarity is largely independent of the particle's lifetime. This is because detecting extra particles can either greatly increase or greatly decrease the effectiveness of an experiment, depending on the experiment's acceptance and the production mechanism of the particle. Therefore, missing energy detection is not a mutually exclusive alternative to the traditional approach of finding decay products, but rather a way to further enhance the sensitivity of an experiment.

While these models can represent a wide range of functions, even those that are computable by a Turing machine may contain non-computable functions. This paper focuses on identifying which functions are computable on infinite inputs, even if those inputs are only partially defined. 

In a previous work, the problem of determining whether a function is computable was linked to the concept of computable selections. A computable selection is a choice of an infinite word from an infinite set of words, also infinite, made by a Turing machine that runs indefinitely. This choice is made for each element of the set, resulting in a final infinite word. 

This paper extends the connection between computable functions and computable selections to include multi-dimensional settings and show that the problem of determinining computability is decidable in these more complex scenarios. 

However, in contrast to one-dimensional words, the relationship between computable functions on infinite words and computable selections is undecidable. This is because a Turing machine that can decide whether a given function is computable would resolve a known undecidability result affecting finite and infinite words. 

As a result, the decision problem for computable instances of (fin)ite words, infinite words, and two-dimensional arrays of infinite words remains undecidable.

Two key theories attempt to explain this animacy continuum: the visual categorization theory proposes that it is driven by the presence of animal-specific characteristics, while the agency theory suggests that it is rooted in how animals are perceived as agents. In this study, we investigated these hypotheses by creating a stimulus set that isolated visual categorizability and agency, and then used fMRI to analyze how they contributed to the animacy continuum in the ventral temporal cortex. Our results indicate that both visual categorizability and agency play distinct roles in shaping the animacy continuum, and that together they fully account for its complexity. omechanical behavior in polymer crystallization. Strain-induced crystallization plays a significant role in polymer mechanical and thermal properties and must be accounted for during production and final product application design. To effectively capture its mechanical and thermal impacts, the proposed model utilizes a unique decomposition approach to the deformation gradient and applies the Coleman--Noll procedure and minimum dissipation potential principle to material modeling. The resulting model includes suitable Helmholtz free energy and dissipation potential assumptions, which enables simulation of crystalline region deformation, melting, and re-crystallization during cyclic loading conditions commonly used in material property measurement. Numerical implementation within a finite element framework allows for simulation of material samples with initially randomised void space, enabling the simulation of crystalline region formation, deformation, and re-crystallization. The developed model has been validated through comparison with experimental results, showing that it accurately captures the complex changes in material during cyclic loading conditions.

For instance, in robotics, guiding a robot through kinesthetic demonstrations is a complex process. The teacher must not only provide correct task-specific state actions but also account for variations in state action spaces that are difficult to formalize. Due to these difficulties, the quality of learned policies is often limited by the quality of demonstrations. To overcome this limitation, researchers have proposed offline imitation learning, which allows them to train a policy using a large dataset of suboptimal demonstrations. However, even this approach is hindered by the presence of corrupted or irrelevant data. To address this issue, this study proposes a novel offline imitation learning algorithm that utilizes state action rewards provided by the teacher as an additional supervision signal. By incorporating this signal, the algorithm can distinguish between relevant and irrelevant data, allowing it to train a high-quality policy using only the relevant data. Theoretical analysis has shown that the algorithm can train a policy that is nearly as good as an optimal policy using a smaller set of relevant data. Experimental results have demonstrated the effectiveness of the algorithm in learning tasks that require kinesthetic demonstrations, outperforming existing baselines by a significant margin.

unclonable encryption, a technique that prevents an adversary from creating multiple ciphertexts decrypting to the same original message. This notion is revisited, and the following points are addressed: 

- Enhancements: Previous constructions either offered one-time security in the plain model or security in the random oracle model. New constructions provide unclonable encryption schemes with semantic security under minimal assumptions, available for both public-key and private-key settings.
- Limitations: The information-theoretic one-time secure construction by Broadbent and Lord was analyzed, revealing a cloning attack with a probability of success of $0.85^n$. A broader class of monogamy of entanglement games is used to generalize the construction, and a $0.75^n$ cloning attack is demonstrated against their scheme.
- Implications: Stronger forms of unclonable encryption imply stronger forms of unclonable encryption for specific types of data, which, in turn, imply stronger forms of unclonable commitments under certain assumptions. Although the current constructions bypass the initial conjecture, it is still unclear whether clonable ciphertexts can be achieved with reasonable security parameters.

By analyzing the anomalous Hall resistance, we found that the spin-orbit proximity effect leads to a notable enhancement of the anomalous Hall resistance in magnetic layers with reduced exchange field. This increase in anomalous Hall resistance is attributed to a substantial enhancement of effective anisotropic Fermi surface warping, which exhibits an exponential dependence on the proximity layer thickness at the exchange-dominated regime. Our findings provide a means to modulate the anomalous Hall resistance in magnetic proximate exchange layers through precise control of the thickness of the proximity layer.

searching for signs of extraterrestrial life through SETI initiatives, with a Dyson Sphere as a primary target - an advanced megastructure capable of harnessing a star's energy for an advanced civilization. An approach to this involves using active measurement tools that employ probes along the network to generate artificial traffic and assess network performance. However, these tools consume considerable resources and typically only cover a small portion of what could be measured, which can lead to missed SLA breaches. The definition of this limited scope is currently the domain of human administrators, who lack the scalability and adaptability needed for dynamic networks. This article explores the potential benefits of employing peer-to-peer (P2P) technology to enhance the detection of SLA breaches. Initially, we outline the principles of steering active measurement tools using P2P technology, which involves decentralized decision-making across a network utilizing probes as decision-making entities. We then examine three strategies for guiding measurement tools, which are based on heuristics, logical conditions, and learning mechanisms. We discuss the limitations of these approaches in handling dynamic networks and propose a strategy that leverages P2P networks to discover SLA breaches more effectively. This strategy involves a more complex learning mechanism that acknowledges the constraints of measurement tools and network administrators, as well as the uncertainty associated with logical conditions and measurement outcomes.

, cutting-edge long-baseline neutrino experiments heavily rely on accurate models of neutrino interactions with atomic nuclei. These models contribute significantly to the overall systematic uncertainty due to the limited ability to reconstruct the final state in neutrino scattering events. The upcoming generation of long-baseline neutrino experiments features near detectors that utilize three-dimensional projection chambers, an innovative technology capable of detailed neutrino event reconstruction by tracing the paths of final state particles and secondary interactions. The initial prototype of such a detector, built at the Brookhaven National Laboratory's neutrino beamline, has undergone neutron and gamma-ray irradiation to simulate neutrino interactions in a functioning state. Following the irradiation, the prototype was exposed to a finely graded neutrino beam to test its capabilities in measuring multiplicities and kinematics of neutrons and protons produced in neutrino interactions. The prototype demonstrated an ability to distinguish between elastic and inelastic neutrino interactions and measured proton multiplicities in inelastic events, aligning with established models of neutrino interactions.

how temperature affects the adhesion between tiny chondritic particles. Our results showed that their surface energy decreased by approximately five times with increasing temperature. In this study, we investigated how the presence of surface water impacts these particles. Typically, laboratory conditions involve drying the particles, but in real-world situations, especially in the inner solar system, water is always present. To account for this, we re-examined our previous data using a model that incorporates water as a separate phase. This model showed that for temperatures below 300 Kelvin, water reduces the tensile strength required for the particles to break apart, but above 300 Kelvin, its effect becomes less significant. This is because water's ability to decrease the particles' sticking together diminishes as temperatures rise. Our findings suggest that even at high temperatures, water still allows the particles to stick together, which is consistent with observations of comets and asteroids that show they can stick together in hot and humid conditions.

Unlike unconstrained methods that neglect environmental and kinematic constraints, constrained imitation learning allows the transfer of human skills to unstructured environments, making it more practical for real-world applications. However, the parabolic model is insufficient for describing polymers grafted to concave or curved surfaces such as spherical particles or interfaces of block copolymers. Previous research has demonstrated that curved, stretched brushes necessitate a boundary layer devoid of free chain ends, requiring modifications to the theoretical analysis. Although the "end exclusion zone" has been successfully integrated into models of brushes on the outer surfaces of cylinders and spheres, the behavior of brushes on surfaces with arbitrary curvature remains unexplored. This study develops a formulation of the strong-stretching theory for molten brushes on surfaces with arbitrary curvature and identifies four distinct regimes where brushes are predicted to exhibit end exclusion zones, including regimes with positive mean curvature and negative Gaussian curvature. By numerically solving the strong-stretching brush equations, we report the predicted scaling of the end exclusion zone size, chain end distribution, chain polarization, and free energy of stretching with mean and Gaussian surface curvatures. These results provide a comprehensive understanding of how brush geometry affects end exclusion zones and exact strong-stretching free energies, which can be applied to model the full range of brush geometries encountered in block copolymer assembly.

Our numerical simulations of extension across pre-existing Proterozoic mobile belts reveal that significant thinning and magmatic activity occurred in the interior regions of the rift system.  As the rift system matured, both thermal and mechanical weakening contributed to significant thickness reduction and extensive magmatism in the regions between the pre-existing Proterozoic mobile belts, now part of the conjugate margins. high energy radiation remains a mystery.  Hadronic radiation from the disks around supermassive black holes, formed when magnetic reconnection amplifies magnetic fields, has been proposed as an explanation.  In a previous study, we found that magnetic reconnection cannot efficiently generate magnetic fields in these disks.  However, in this paper we consider an alternative mechanism, known as turbulence-driven reconnection, which may more effectively amplify magnetic fields.  We use this mechanism to calculate the gamma-ray emission from the disks around supermassive blackholes in galaxies, and find that it exceeds the observed radiation threshold.  Furthermore, we discover that if magnetic reconnection in these disks is primarily driven by turbulence, it could be the main source of gamma-ray radiation in the centers of galaxies.

By establishing essential mathematical formulas and developing efficient algorithms rooted in computational geometry and spline theory, we can calculate the probability density function, cumulative distribution function, and k-th moment of the probability function quickly, efficiently, taking advantage of modern computer capabilities. cardiac auscultation is a vital point-of-care method. However, the automatic analysis of heart sounds faces significant challenges due to noise and sensor degradation. This study aims to enhance the accuracy of cardiac auscultation for early heart condition detection in noisy recordings from various sensors. A thorough analysis of existing approaches reveals that feature extraction methods are particularly susceptible to errors. To address this, a comprehensive deep learning network, the Convolutional Neural Network (CNN), is proposed. The network consists of two segments: one for noise reduction and feature extraction, and another for heart sound classification. The U-Net structure is employed to extract relevant information from raw signal time-frequency features, eliminating the need for pre-processing. The network is trained and tested on a publicly available dataset, yielding impressive results when compared to conventional methods. The proposed solution demonstrates robustness across different recordings, paving the way for the development of accurate and portable cardiac auscultation systems for early heart condition detection.

research focuses on the process of producing leptoquark pairs at the Large Hadron Collider with an emphasis on its full complement of production and decay interactions. A leptoquark pair produced through squark-antiquark collisions can result in various outcomes such as four-lepton, two leptons in combination with missing transverse energy, or two jets along with missing transverse energy, depending on the leptoquark's helicity and the chosen production and decay modes. Furthermore, certain leptoquark decays can lead to distinctive signatures like long-lived particles or light scatters, which can also contribute to the detection of leptoquarks. We have developed optimized event selection criteria based on the general purpose ATLAS detector simulation and have analyzed the prospective sensitivity of the search for leptoquark pairs at 13 TeV with an integrated luminosity of 300 inverse femtobarns, specifically focusing on the production of second-generation leptoquarks and various third-generation leptoquarks that undergo decay into quarks and neutrinos or heavy quarks and charged leptons.

Building on the foundation established by Pearl (2009) and Burt et al. (2021a) within the context of parametric models, we extend their framework to cover parametriable models, including the key components of causal deep learning networks. We then employ this comprehensive framework to examine a wide range of parametriable models, including those with latent variables and multiplicative connections, which are also prevalent in causal deep learning architectures. A Newton-Krylov method is employed to solve this system, where BDDC/AMG solvers accelerate the solution process. To ensure a fair comparison, we thoroughly examined the performance of a wide range of solver parameters, including those influencing BDDC/AMG and the nonlinear iteration. Our primary findings are presented in the form of summary statistics, which reveal notable differences in solution times for various cardiac mechanics simulations, with some cases solved up to 7.5 times faster using BDDC. Research has shown that the $2k$th moment of the limit distribution can be directly linked to non-crossing pair-partitions of the set $\{1, 2, \ldots, 2k\}$. This finding has been extended in various studies, and the present paper aims to provide a comprehensive overview of the results (including some new findings) related to limit distributions of standardized Wigner matrices. The study reveals that the moments of the limit distribution are determined by non-crossing partitions of the set of moments, with each partition corresponding to a specific moment formula. The presented partitions encompass not only the classical pair-partitions (as seen in the literature on the semi-circular distribution) but also higher-order partitions, allowing for an in-depth exploration of the limiting behavior of spectra and singular values in multiple contexts, such as random matrices with independent entries, those with independent symmetric entries, and those that factorize, including GUE, GSE, and BAIII.

However, acoustic metagratings have inherent limitations due to their size constraint, which is typically around a wavelength. This limitation hinders their ability to produce high-resolution images. To overcome this limitation, researchers suggest using subwavelength artificial media, but its practical implementation is yet to be demonstrated. In this study, we introduce a novel concept called an acoustic spatial carver that can manipulate subwavelength-sized propagating and reflected waves. Unlike traditional metagratings, this device can control the direction of reflected waves even when they are subwavelength in size. To achieve this, we propose using an acoustic spatial carver based on a nonreciprocal acoustic circulator, which is realized using a chiral fluid with a very small anisotropy parameter. This device has potential to enhance reflection efficiency and enable subwavelength wave manipulation, ultimately contributing to breakthroughs in high-frequency ultrasound imaging and other applications requiring subwavelength wave control.

To illustrate the efficacy of our approach, we applied it to a diverse range of examples and benchmarks, including those featuring intricate reordering paths and safety properties expressed as quantitative temporal safety properties.

What's surprising is that these disks are both inactive and severely uneven in terms of their mass distribution. This suggests that these galaxies are undergoing a process similar to that which occurs in spiral galaxies like the Milky Way, but on a much larger scale. As a result, the central core is actively star-forming, while the outer regions remain inactive. We propose that the suppression of star formation in the outer disks is likely due to the lack of a significant gas reservoir, which we observe in a separate study. Furthermore, we speculate that the distinct unevenness of the disks may be a result of the galaxies' interaction with the surrounding hot gas, which causes matter to clump together in a process known as "strangulation."

rotation pattern within a relatively small and less luminous giant star. Typically, stars with moderate mass exhibit rigid rotation during their main sequence phase. However, as these stars mature into giants, their core shrinks and their outer layers expand, leading to a rotation profile with a rapidly spinning core and a slower surface. Contrary to this expected pattern, observations of KIC 9267654 suggest its outer layers rotate faster than its core, contradicting conventional theories of angular momentum conservation. To resolve this discrepancy, we refined the measurements of the star's surface rotation, confirmed that its pulsation frequencies align with previously established core and envelope rotation rates, and ruled out significant mass loss or interaction with a companion. Furthermore, we eliminated alternative explanations such as magnetic braking or angular momentum redistribution caused by magnetic winds or magnetic reconnection. Instead, we propose that KIC 9267654 may be an intermediate case for angular momentum conservation during the evolution of stars, and also highlights the need for more detailed models of rotation in low-mass giants.

By placing phosphorus dopants in silicon with precise atomic positioning, researchers can study the distinct effects resulting from the competition between these two interactions.
However, these dopants rely on wave functions that are sensitive to the symmetries of silicon's crystal bands, and their placement near gap states makes them prone to lattice imperfections and disorder.
To address these challenges, researchers have proposed placing dopants on the surface of silicon within a He-Ne buffer layer, where they can study the unique physics of quantum tunneling while being relatively insensitive to lattice defects.
By utilizing scanning tunneling microscopy and theoretical calculations, researchers have demonstrated the ability to create a quantized valley current mediated by the envelope function of the dopants and achieved high placement precision of less than 0.5 Angstroms.
The valley current associated with dopants placed in silicon's extended states can exceed 10 electrons/second by adjusting the lattice position to within 0.5 Angstroms, and it is anticipated that this approach could lead to the creation of defect-based quantum valves and other novel devices that utilize tunneling and interactions between silicon defects.

Laser Interstitial Thermal Therapy (LITT) treats seizures caused by epilepsy in a specific brain area, the mesial temporal lobe. To help doctors accurately treat this condition, researchers developed a computational model that uses MRI images to pinpoint the therapy area in detail. Despite recent advancements in deep learning technology, training these models can be difficult due to limited data availability. A new technique called Domain Randomization (DR) offers a solution by simulating various MRI images based on real ones, allowing the model to learn from a wide range of scenarios. However, DR has a major drawback: it's not clear how to create realistic simulated images that accurately reflect the underlying structure of real images, using a type of image called a encoder. A new approach called Contrast-Invariant Training (CIT) addresses this issue by modifying the DR process to focus on learning the distinct features of different scenarios while preserving the unique patterns within each image. The researchers applied this new technique to LITT therapy planning and showed that it significantly improves the accuracy of model predictions when testing it with real data.

Parkinson's disease, a neurodegenerative disorder, results from the death of dopaminergic neurons in the substantia nigra, disrupting the basal ganglia-thalamus-cortex circuit. Despite multiple contributing factors, a comprehensive understanding of the disease's mechanisms remains elusive, and no cure exists. In response, researchers employ computational models that mimic Parkinson's Disease pathophysiology and neural circuitry to explore disease causes and potential treatments. Our model consists of a four-layer mesoscopic neural network model featuring conductance-based excitatory and inhibitory neurons. It was trained and validated using multiple frequency local field potential signals from three Parkinson's Disease relevant brain regions: the putamen, substantia nigra, and primary motor cortex. The model successfully replicated distinct frequency patterns observed in healthy and Parkinson's Disease animal brains. By incorporating dopamine modulation, the model recreated decreased dopamine levels characteristic of Parkinson's Disease, leading to impaired cognitive function. Notably, our model offers a potential explanation for the rotation threshold hypothesis, a prominent theory in Parkinson's Disease's motor symptoms.

Traditionally, this relies on having access to the original network's training data and parameters, which isn't always feasible due to storage or privacy constraints in real-world applications. This study introduces decision-based black-box knowledge distillation, allowing a model to be trained on the behavior of a network whose internal workings are inaccessible, as long as it produces classification decisions. When access to the original data is possible, a training sample's resistance to other classes is quantified by measuring the distance between its decision and the midpoint of other classes' decisions. This is used to create a soft label for each data point, which the model is trained to match. When access to the original data isn't possible, pseudo soft labels are derived from the empirical distribution of the logistic regression decision values on the inaccessible network. Our proposed approach is evaluated on multiple networks and datasets, showing that it can achieve comparable performance to traditional knowledge distillation methods. Furthermore, it demonstrates the potential for models to be trained on inaccessible networks even when no training data is available, a true black-box scenario.

Given a graph~$G$ and an integer~$k$, the Strong Geodetic problem asks whether there exists a subset of vertices in~$G$ with at most~$k$ vertices, which is strong geodetic. To address this issue, we introduce Co-Imitation Learning (CoIL), a novel framework that enables agents to learn from each other's past experiences without expert supervision. However, recent findings suggest that this approach may merely build upon the pre-trained token embeddings, implying a limited scope for reinforcement learning to explore new representation spaces. This study investigates the role of pre-trained token and sentence representations in sequential reinforcement learning for NMT. We demonstrate that pre-training sentence representations enhances RL's translation quality gains, while pre-training token representations is counterproductive if RL is applied to the token-level. Moreover, our analysis reveals that RL with the general learned sentence representations outperforms task-specific pre-trained representations, as validated by quantitative and qualitative results showing improved paraphrasing abilities. These discoveries indicate that the effectiveness of RL in NMT heavily relies on the interplay between token and sentence representations.

In this context, we explore how the Peccei-Quinn symmetry breaking affects neutrino properties at the one-loop level. As a result, we find that the axion's decay constant can be influenced by neutrino interactions with axions and dark matter, leading to significant implications for neutrino masses and oscillation lengths. We establish the relationship between the axion's decay constant and neutrino masses, finding that a typical value of $f_\gamma \approx 10^{10}\,{\rm Sm}$ implies that neutrino masses lie within the sub-eV range. This framework also provides a theoretical explanation for the small neutrino masses through the Witten effect, resulting in a minimum neutrino mass of approximately $10^{-14}\,{\rm eV}$. Furthermore, we discover that neutrino masses directly impact the axion's two-body decay into a photon and a neutrino, leading to the conclusion that present-day searches for axion decay into neutrinos have already probed neutrino masses in the $10^{-20}\,{\rm eV}$ range.

To address this issue, researchers have been exploring debiased models, but the problem remains complex due to the inherent difficulty in identifying and removing implicit biases. To overcome this challenge, Dr. Li and colleagues propose a novel framework that not only learns a model free from explicit and implicit biases but also capable of identifying and removing implicit biases in medical image datasets. The framework consists of three primary components: a classifier, a bias detector, and a bias correction module. The classifier is trained to minimize explicit and implicit biases while being robust to distributional changes; the bias detector identifies regions with potential explicit and implicit biases; and the bias correction module actively removes these biases. The proposed framework has been validated through experiments on multiple datasets, showcasing its effectiveness in eliminating explicit and implicit biases and improving model robustness. The authors also provide insights into the types of explicit biases that can be learned by deep models, and their work has the potential to be applied to other challenging problems in medical machine learning.

These flybys occurred close to Jupiter's magnetic field and allowed us to analyze energy flux variations. Our findings show that the solar wind energy flux on Io's orbit is around 100 watts per square meter, which is significantly higher than the flux on more distant moons. This increase in energy flux is attributed to the higher electron flux and the presence of accelerated electrons near Jupiter's magnetic field. On Io, we observed a correlation between the solar wind energy flux and electron flux, but not with the solar wind speed. In contrast, on the more distant moons, we found no correlation between the solar wind energy flux and electron flux. Our results suggest that enhanced electron flux contributes to the sputtering of these moons' surfaces and may have implications for the formation of magnetospheric environments and the sputtering rates of airless bodies in the solar system.

In contrast, our research extends this understanding by exploring ensembles of LDPC codes that exhibit degree-degree correlations. We developed two methods to construct correlated LDPC code ensembles, derived a density evolution (DE) framework applicable to binary erasure channels, and through extensive simulations, we investigated the impact of degree-degree correlations on LDPC code performance. Our key findings include: (1) positively correlated LDPC codes can achieve superior error rates, even when uncorrelated codes with identical degree distributions perform poorly; (2) negatively correlated LDPC codes may exhibit poor performance, but certain negative correlations can enhance error rate resistance; and (3) degree-degree correlations can significantly influence LDPC code performance, even when the connected component degree distributions are uncorrelated and satisfy standard stability criteria.

As a result, the proposed remedy may inadvertently enable a successful attack, also known as the "hacking threat" in QKD. To address this issue, researchers have suggested alternative protocols that can prevent hacking, but these solutions come with decreased key rates, making them impractical. This study aims to overcome this limitation by developing a novel decoder strategy for the vacuum+weak decoy state method that can detect an eavesdropper without compromising key rates. To achieve this, we introduce a decoder based on error rates in the weak state, rather than the vacuum state, and demonstrate its effectiveness using realistic parameters from state-of-the-art QKD systems. Our results indicate that this decoder can safely store approximately 68.5% of initial keys when source phase fluctuates by 10 degrees, and it can detect eavesdropping even when phase fluctuations increase to 20 degrees with only a minimal reduction in key rates.

This approach involves utilizing two distinct types of Hamiltonians: a driver Hamiltonian and a problem Hamiltonian. By gradually transitioning from the driver Hamiltonian to the problem Hamiltonian, it is possible to achieve the target ground state that represents the solution to the problem. Research suggests that incorporating non-stoquastic terms into the driver Hamiltonian may enhance the efficiency of quantum annealing, but it is also hampered by decoherence. However, a recent study reveals that non-stoquastic Hamiltonians can lead to catastrophic failure of quantum annealing, even when decoherence is minimal. This counterintuitive finding is attributed to the unphysical nature of non-stoquastic Hamiltonians, which causes quantum annealing to collapse in a way that is difficult to understand. The study also presents a criterion for avoiding this failure and explores its implications for driver Hamiltonians that are not exactly known.

As a leading research institution founded by Jacobus Cornelius Kapteyn, the laboratory was working on Kapteyn's Plan of Selected Areas when van Rhijn took over. Van Rhijn's research was thorough but lacked a broader perspective, failing to connect his findings to the emerging understanding of the galaxy and its structure. The laboratory's future development and the research it conducted during this period are examined in detail, providing a comprehensive overview of the institution's activities.

These composites possess an intrinsic ability to detect damage through changes in electrical conductivity, known as piezoresistivity. Researchers have successfully leveraged this property to develop damage detection methods, such as electrical resistance change techniques and imaging methods like electrical impedance tomography (EIT). However, these methods are limited in their ability to provide detailed information about damage type, size, and location. To overcome this limitation, scientists have explored the use of machine learning algorithms on conductivity measurements to identify damage in composites, but these methods are hindered by a lack of physically based understanding and large numbers of necessary measurements. To address this challenge, a machine learning model called siNNs was created that detects damage in carbon nanofiber-reinforced composites by utilizing a physically inspired approach and requiring fewer measurements than traditional methods. When tested on measurements obtained from a mechanical testing setup, siNNs was able to accurately determine the size and shape of damage in composites, demonstrating its potential to enhance the accuracy of damage size estimation for self-sensing composite structures.

A comprehensive dataset was collected from 70 online learning modules in both the Fall 2020 and Spring 2020 semesters, with the first 41 modules assigned before campus closure. Three key metrics measured students' ability to stay on track: timely submission, early submission for extra credit, and engagement with modules. These findings suggest that remote learning had a detrimental effect on first-generation students' ability to keep up with coursework and a positive impact on URM students.

Within Toda conformal field theories, this higher-spin symmetry is made apparent through a Lie algebra based on simple roots, in contrast to the spin-3/2 representation seen in Liouville. Although this symmetry is initially evident at the level of primary fields, it extends to all fields within the theory, as demonstrated by a recent finding that a specific higher-spin current lies within the descent equations' kernel. By applying a four-dimensional perspective, we derive higher-spin symmetry in two dimensions through a spin-anomalous dimension, analogous to how it appears in three dimensions as a result of the Wess-Zumino term. computational challenges when dealing with large-scale linear systems and matrix inversion. To address this issue, researchers have been exploring fast approximate iterative matrix inversion methods, leveraging Graphical Processing Unit (GPU) acceleration. Recent studies have focused on methods such as Neumann Series, Newton iteration, and Chebyshev Iteration, among others. In this work, we introduce a novel iterative algorithm called 'Nested Neumann' (NN), which builds upon the Neumann Series and generalizes higher-order iterations like Newton and Chebyshev. The NN method benefits from a computationally free iterative update of the preconditioning matrix, utilizing an inception depth parameter. Theoretical analysis has shown that NN converges under specific conditions, achieves a convergence rate equivalent to its inception depth plus one, and has an optimal inception depth of one or two, depending on available RAM. We also derive an explicit formula for the NN, applicable to massive sparse matrices through an approximation technique. Notably, the NN method can produce an approximate inverse matrix in a form that is itself sparse, even when dealing with large sparse linear systems. We have benchmarked the NN on various systems, including the famous FEM benchmark, showcasing the NN's performance on different GPUs and benchmarking systems.

As the number of blockchain users continues to rise, so too will the frequency and severity of these attacks. Given the growing problem, it is essential to develop effective methods for detecting malicious behavior on blockchain networks. This paper presents a novel approach that utilizes machine learning to identify suspicious transactions based on contextual information from blockchain data.
